Improvise over a blues backing, step by step
Learn to improvise on the 12-bar blues, in one key at a time. Start the backing track, pick a step, and play along. Everything is written for your alto.
Chords written for alto, bar by bar. Shaded bars: listen or rest in this step.
The fourth note is the blue note: slide through it, do not sit on it.
These steps follow common advice from saxophone and jazz teachers: blues first, one key, few notes, rhythm and space, call and response, target notes, motifs, and learning solos by ear.
Just listen to a few choruses. Count 4 beats in each bar and follow the bars on screen: the chord moves up in bar 5, comes home in bar 7, and the tension peaks in bar 9 before the turnaround.
Improvise with just the three notes shown. With so few notes, all your attention goes to rhythm: short and long notes, repeated notes, starting off the beat. Leave gaps.
The backing plays a short phrase in bars 1–2, 5–6 and 9–10. Answer it in the next two bars: first copy it by ear, then answer with your own phrase that sounds related.
Now use all six notes of the blues scale. Know them by heart before you play, and keep the rhythm ideas from the three-note step.
Play for two bars, then stay silent for two bars, all the way through. The silences turn notes into phrases and give you time to hear what comes next.
On each chord change, land on the note shown (the chord\'s 3rd), on a strong beat. Approach it from the note just above or below. Your solo will start to follow the chords.
Pick a short idea of 3 to 5 notes. Play it, then play it again changing one thing only: its rhythm, its last note, or the beat it starts on. Keep it recognisable through the whole chorus.

Pick a sax solo you love in the song player. Loop two bars, slow them down, sing them, then find them on the sax. Phrase by phrase, then play along at full speed: this is how most players build their vocabulary.
Name as many notes as you can in one minute. Best score per level.
Five notes that always sound right over the blues: the three you know plus two more. Learn them by heart, up and down, then improvise with them using the rhythms and gaps from the earlier steps.
A brighter, sweeter sound than the blues scale. Try it over the first four bars, then mix it with the minor pentatonic and hear how the mood changes.
The backing starts again from bar 1 and the microphone records you. Headphones keep the backing out of the recording.
